claim_text: The main goal of the SELF-RAG framework is to enhance the quality and factuality of Language Models (LLMs) by using retrieval on demand and self-reflection.

It trains an LM to learn to retrieve, generate, and critique text passages and its own generation by predicting the next tokens from its original vocabulary as well as newly added special tokens, called reflection tokens.
SELF-RAG further enables the tailoring of LM behaviors at test time by leveraging reflection tokens.
This work demonstrates that SELF-RAG significantly outperforms LLMs with more parameters or with conventional retrieval-augmented generation approaches.
The special tokens introduced by SELF-RAG are called reflection tokens.

Their purpose is to enable the model to learn to retrieve, generate, and critique text passages and its own generation by predicting the next tokens from its original vocabulary as well as these newly added special tokens.
These reflection tokens further enable the tailoring of the model's behaviors at test time by leveraging them.
SELF-RAG decides whether retrieval is necessary during generation by using a special token called "Retrieve."
If the model determines that the sequence does not require factual grounding or may not be enhanced by knowledge retrieval, the "Retrieve" token is set to "No."
If the model determines that retrieval is necessary, the "Retrieve" token is set to "Yes."
The model then retrieves the top K passages, and for each passage, it further evaluates whether the passage is relevant and predicts "Relevant" or "Irrelevant."
If a passage is relevant, the model further evaluates whether the passage supports the model generation and predicts "Fully supported," "Partially supported," or "No support."

The three aspects of retrieved passages that the critic evaluates in the SELF-RAG framework are:
Relevance (ISREL): This evaluates whether the passage provides useful information to solve the given problem or question.
Support (ISSUP): This evaluates whether all the verification-worthy statements in the generated response are supported by the retrieved passage.
This evaluates the overall utility of the generated response, considering both relevance and support.
These evaluations help SELF-RAG to generate more accurate and useful responses by carefully selecting generations based on fine-grained multiple criteria.
The language model used to initialize the critic model during SELF-RAG training was the same one as the generator LM.
SELF-RAG differs from conventional RAG systems in deciding when to retrieve documents by incorporating a model (M) that decodes a retrieval token to evaluate the utility of retrieval.
If retrieval is not required, the model predicts the next output segment as it does in a standard Language Model (LM).

If retrieval is needed, the model generates a critique token to evaluate the retrieved passage's relevance, the next response segment, and another critique token to evaluate if the information in the response segment is supported by the passage.
Finally, a new critique token evaluates the overall utility of the response.
This approach allows SELF-RAG to process multiple passages in parallel and use its own generated reflection tokens to enforce soft constraints or hard control over the generated task output.

The critic model in SELF-RAG plays a role in constructing the training data for the generator by predicting the next tokens from the original vocabulary as well as newly added special tokens, called reflection tokens.
These reflection tokens are used to critique the text passages and the generator's own generation.
The critic model helps the generator to learn to retrieve, generate, and critique text passages, thereby enhancing the quality and factuality of the LLMs.
The SELF-RAG generator learns to produce both normal text and reflection tokens through a training process that involves two models: the critic model (C) and the generator model (M).
Training the Critic Model (C): The critic model is trained on a curated corpus with interleaving passages retrieved by a retriever and reflection tokens predicted by the critic model itself.
The critic model's goal is to evaluate the utility of retrieved passages and the quality of a given task output.
Training the Generator Model (M): The generator model M is trained on the same curated corpus as the critic model, but it learns to predict the target output as well as the reflection tokens.
During training, the retrieved text chunks are masked out for loss calculation, and the original vocabulary is expanded with a set of reflection tokens {Critique, Retrieve}.
The generator model learns to generate reflection tokens by itself without relying on the critic at inference time.

In essence, the SELF-RAG generator is designed to decide when to retrieve information, evaluate the utility of retrieved passages, and generate both the response and reflection tokens for that response.
This allows the model to produce more accurate and contextually relevant responses.

After the critic determines that a retrieved passage is relevant to the generated response, the model generates a critique token to evaluate if the information in the response segment is supported by the passage.
If the information is supported, the model generates the next response segment.
If not, the model may continue to retrieve and evaluate additional passages until a supported response is generated.
This process continues until the model generates a response that is deemed useful and supported by the available passages.

Instead, Figure 3(a) shows the performance of RAG-Token and RAG-Sequence models as more documents are retrieved, with no specific comparison to other variants.
The retrieval frequency dramatically changes when the retrieval threshold is increased, as shown in Figure 3(c).
The model retrieves less as the threshold increases.
Increasing the amount of training data significantly improves SELF-RAG's performance on PopQA and ASQA, while no significant improvements are observed on PubHealth.
This information can be inferred from the context on pages 9 and 10 of the document "Self-RAG.pdf".
The figures mentioned are not explicitly provided, but the performance analysis on different amounts of training data is described in detail.

Increasing the retrieval threshold creates a trade-off between retrieval frequency and model performance because, with a higher threshold, the model retrieves less often, which may lead to a decrease in model performance due to less available information.
However, on some datasets like PubHealth, the performance drop by retrieving less is smaller compared to others like PopQA.
This information is found on page 9 of the document "SELF-RAG.pdf" in the context provided.

SELF-RAG can outperform conventional retrieval-augmented models on tasks where the answer cannot simply be copied from retrieved passages because it uses a self-reflection mechanism that allows the model to evaluate the relevance, support, and completeness of the generated output and the retrieved passages.
This mechanism enables the model to make more informed decisions about when and how to use the retrieved passages, resulting in more accurate and relevant responses.

In contrast, conventional retrieval-augmented models may indiscriminately use retrieved passages without ensuring complete support from the cited sources, leading to less accurate and relevant responses.

The name Donut stands for "Document Understanding Transformer".
The model is designed to solve the problem of visual document understanding without relying on OCR (Optical Character Recognition) and can be trained in an end-to-end manner.

The main problems associated with OCR-dependent Visual Document Understanding (VDU) methods, as per the provided context, are:
High computational costs due to the use of OCR.
Inflexibility of OCR models on languages or types of documents.
OCR error propagation to the subsequent process.
These issues are addressed by the proposed OCR-free Document Understanding Transformer model, which aims to model a direct mapping from a raw input image to the desired output without relying on OCR.

Donut uses a Swin Transformer as its visual encoder in the experiments.
Donut uses the BART (Denoising Autoencoder for Retrieval and Translation) decoder to convert visual features into structured information.

Information flows through Donut as follows:
The input document image is processed by the visual encoder, which converts it into a set of embeddings.
In this study, Swin Transformer is used as the encoder network.
The encoded embeddings are then fed into the textual decoder, which maps the derived features into a sequence of subword tokens.
The sequence of subword tokens is used to construct a desired structured format, such as JSON.
Each model component is Transformer-based, allowing for easy end-to-end training.
The final structured output is the answer to the question posed, in the format specified by the question.
In the example provided, the question is "what is the price of choco mochi?", and the final structured output is the price, formatted as "14,000".
Donut does not rely on any modules related to OCR functionality, but it uses a visual encoder for extracting features from the given document image.
This makes it an end-to-end (self-contained) VDU model for general understanding of document images.
Donut does not require an OCR module because it models a direct mapping from a raw input image to the desired output without OCR.

This is done by using a visual encoder for extracting features from a given document image, and a textual decoder for mapping the derived features into a sequence of subword tokens to construct a desired structured format.
(Donut.pdf, Page 2, 4, 9, 11)
Donut's pre-training process teaches the model to read text from document images by predicting the next words by conditioning jointly on the image and previous text contexts.
During the pre-training phase, Donut learns how to read the texts using a Transformer-based visual encoder and is pre-trained with document images and their text annotations.
The pre-training objective is simple, allowing for domain and language flexibility, and can be realized straightforwardly by pre-training with synthetic data.
The SynthDoG synthetic document generator is used to generate samples for pre-training a document understanding model.
It is built using the Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and English Wikipedia, and follows the image rendering pipeline of Yim et al.
The generated samples play an important role in the pre-training of the Donut model.
Details of SynthDoG can be found in the code and Appendix A.2 of the document.

Donut outperforms OCR-dependent VDU models in terms of memory usage (91M vs. Not specified in the provided documents), inference time (0.6 sec vs. Not specified in the provided documents), and accuracy (0.8% vs. Not specified in the provided documents).

Donut converts a document image into a structured JSON-like output through the following process:
Visual Encoder: The input document image is first converted into a set of embeddings by the visual encoder.
This encoder can be a CNN-based model, Transformer-based model, or in this study, Swin Transformer is used due to its best performance in preliminary studies.

Swin Transformer splits the input image into non-overlapping patches, applies Swin Transformer blocks (consisting of a shifted window-based multi-head self-attention module and a two-layer MLP), and patch merging layers at each stage.
The output of the final Swin Transformer block is fed into the textual decoder.
Textual Decoder: The output of the final Swin Transformer block is fed into the textual decoder.
The decoder maps the derived features into a sequence of subword tokens to construct a desired structured format, such as JSON.
Each model component is Transformer-based.
Output Conversion: The output token sequence is converted to a desired structured format, such as JSON.
Special tokens like [START *] and
[END *] are added to the sequence, where * indicates each field to extract.
If the output token sequence is wrongly structured, the field is treated as lost.
In summary, Donut directly maps an input document image into a desired structured output without relying on any modules related to OCR functionality.
The output is in the form of a JSON-like structure.

The paper argues that Donut's OCR-free approach can be advantageous for multilingual document understanding and real-world deployment due to several reasons.
First, it eliminates the need for retraining an off-the-shelf OCR engine for different languages or domain changes, which can be expensive and inflexible.
Second, it addresses the issue of OCR error propagation to subsequent processes, which can occur in OCR-based approaches.
Lastly, it is cost-effective since it reduces the computational cost for inference compared to high-quality OCR results.
The main purpose of LayoutLMv3 is to introduce a multimodal model in Document AI that does not rely on a pre-trained CNN or Faster R-CNN backbone to extract visual features.
This is aimed to significantly save parameters and eliminate complex pre-processing steps, which is vital to Document AI models.

The problem it aims to address in Document AI pre-training is the reliance on complex pre-trained CNN or Faster R-CNN backbones for visual feature extraction, which can be resource-intensive and complex.
The three pre-training objectives used by LayoutLMv3 are:
Masked Language Modeling (MLM): This objective learns the language representation by masking 30% of text tokens and predicting them from the context.
Masked Image Modeling (MIM): This objective learns the image representation by masking out a portion of input image patches and reconstructing them in the output.
This helps in preserving the image information until the last layer of the model.
Word-Patch Alignment (WPA): This objective learns cross-modal alignment by predicting whether the corresponding image patch of a text word is masked.
This helps in learning the relationship between text and image.
Each objective learns a different aspect of the multimodal representation, either text, image, or the relationship between them.
LayoutLMv3 avoids using a pre-trained CNN or Faster R-CNN backbone for extracting visual features because it aims to significantly save parameters and eliminate region annotations.
This design choice makes the model simpler and easier to reproduce.

LayoutLMv3 represents document images by resizing them into a specific size, splitting the image into a sequence of uniform patches, linearly projecting the image patches to a certain dimension, and flattening them into a sequence of vectors.
This method is inspired by Vision Transformer (ViT) and ViLT.
The image patches are then fed into the multimodal Transformer for further processing.
The text representation in LayoutLMv3 consists of two types of embeddings: word-level spatial embeddings and embeddings of BERT.
LayoutLMv3 uses segment-level 2D positions, while LayoutLM and LayoutLMv2 use word-level layout positions.
The use of segment-level positions in LayoutLMv3 means that words in a segment share the same 2D position since the words usually express the same semantic meaning.
This change may benefit the semantic entity labeling task on FUNSD, making LayoutLMv3 and the other works using word-level positions not directly comparable.
The text tokens and image patches are combined by taking the linear projection of patches and word tokens as inputs and encoding them into contextualized vector representations.
The image patches are first resized and split into a sequence of uniform P x P patches, linearly projected to D dimensions, and flattened into a sequence of vectors.
The text tokens are embedded using word embedding layers.
The resulting sequences of text and image vectors are then fed into the multimodal Transformer for processing.
The purpose of the Word-Patch Alignment (WPA) objective in LayoutLMv3 is to learn a fine-grained alignment between text words and image patches in documents.
This objective is proposed to facilitate cross-modal representation learning and improve the performance of both text-centric and image-centric tasks in Document AI.

Masked Image Modeling (MIM) in LayoutLMv3 differs from reconstructcting raw image pixels as it preserves the image information until the last layer of the model by randomly masking out a portion of input image patches and reconstructing them in the output.
This approach allows the model to learn rich visual representations without directly dealing with raw image pixels.

LayoutLMv3's image embedding approach differs from the CNN/grid and region-feature approaches used by models such as DocFormer and SelfDoc in that it learns visual models from scratch via natural language supervision and does not densely connect the two domains with a joint attention model.
The only interaction in a LayoutLMv3 model between the image and text domain is a single dot product in a learned joint embedding space.

In contrast, models like DocFormer and SelfDoc use convolutional neural networks (CNN) to extract grid or region features from images, and these features are then used in conjunction with text features for downstream tasks.
Adding MIM and WPA to the LayoutLMv3 model significantly improves the performance on the PubLayNet dataset compared to MLM-only models.
Specifically, the model with MIM and WPA (model #4) achieves a higher mAP score (89.78) compared to the model with only MLM (model #1, 88.64).
The incorporation of MIM and WPA objectives also helps in regularizing the training and decreasing the loss, as shown in Figure 4.

The five benchmark datasets used to evaluate LayoutLMv3 are:
RVL-CDIP: This dataset is used for the document image classification task, which aims to predict the category of document images.

PubLayNet: This dataset is used for document layout understanding tasks, containing research paper images annotated with bounding boxes and polygonal segmentation across five document layout categories: text, title, list, figure, and table.
This dataset is used for the document visual question answering task, which requires a model to take a document image and a question as input and output an answer.
FUNSD: This dataset is used for semantic entity labeling tasks on documents.
This dataset is used for named entity recognition and coreference resolution tasks on documents.
Each dataset represents a different type of Document AI task.
BLIP-2 aims to solve the problem of vision-language pre-training by bridging the modality gap between frozen pre-trained image encoders and large language models (LLMs).
The Q-Former, a proposed trainable module, addresses this problem by extracting a fixed number of output features from the image encoder, which are then used by the LLM to output the desired text.

This is achieved through a two-stage pre-training procedure: (1) vision-language representation learning, where the Q-Former learns visual representation most relevant to the text, and (2) vision-to-language generative learning, where the Q-Former's output visual representation is interpreted by the LLM.
The Q-Former consists of two transformer submodules that share the same self-attention layers, with one submodule interacting with the frozen image encoder.
The two stages of BLIP-2's pre-training procedure are:
First stage: Pre-training for 250k steps with a batch size of 2320/1680 for ViT-L/ViT-g and a batch size of 1920/1520 for OPT/FlanT5.
Second stage: Pre-training for 80k steps with the same batch sizes as the first stage.
During this stage, the learning rate is adjusted with a cosine decay and a minimum learning rate of 5e-5.
The two Transformer submodules that make up the Q-Former are the Image Encoder and the Language Model (LLM).
The Image Encoder extracts visual features from the input image and converts it into a sequence of patch embeddings.
The LLM receives these output patch embeddings and the question as input, and predicts answers.
The question is also provided as a condition to the Image Encoder, such that the extracted image features are more relevant to the question.
The Q-Former is a trainable module designed to bridge the gap between a frozen image encoder and a frozen Large Language Model (LLM).
It extracts a fixed number of output features from the image encoder, which are then used by the LLM to generate texts.
The Q-Former consists of two transformer submodules that share the same self-attention layers: an image transformer and a text transformer.
The image transformer interacts with the frozen image encoder, while the text transformer interacts with the LLM.
The queries in the image transformer interact with each other, with the frozen image features, and with the text through self-attention layers.
The queries are forced to extract visual features that capture all the information about the text.

During pre-training, the Q-Former goes through two stages:
Vision-Language Representation Learning:
In this stage, the Q-Former is connected to a frozen image encoder, and pre-training is performed using image-text pairs.
The goal is to train the Q-Former such that the queries can learn to extract visual representation that is most informative of the text.

In this stage, the output of the Q-Former is connected to a frozen LLM, and the Q-Former is trained such that its output visual representation can be interpreted by the LLM.
The Q-Former is initialized with the pre-trained weights of BERT base, while the cross-attention layers are randomly initialized.
In total, Q-Former contains 188M parameters.
The document does not provide specific information about the number of learnable query embeddings used by the Q-Former or the dimensionality of each query.

However, it mentions that the resulting sequence of embedding vectors serves as input to the encoder, which suggests that the number of embeddings would be equal to the number of input images or patches.
The dimensionality of each embedding could be inferred from the specific model architecture being used, but it is not explicitly stated in the provided document.
The Q-Former contains approximately 1.3 billion parameters, which is relatively lightweight compared to the large language models used by BLIP-2.

The reason for this is that the Q-Former is designed to be efficient and focused on learning to bridge the modality gap between images and language, rather than being a general-purpose language model.
This allows it to have fewer parameters while still achieving strong performance in vision-to-language tasks.

The three objectives used during the first-stage vision-language representation learning of BLIP-2 are:
Pre-training the Q-Former to learn visual features relevant to the text.
Reducing the burden of the LLM to learn vision-language alignment.
Mitigating the catastrophic forgetting problem by effectively functioning as an information bottleneck that feeds the most useful information to the LLM while removing irrelevant visual information.
Image-Text Contrastive Learning (ITC) determines the similarity between an image and its corresponding text by maximizing the mutual information between their representations.
It contrasts the image-text similarity of a positive pair against those of negative pairs.
The output query representation Z from the image transformer is aligned with the text representation from the text transformer.
The [CLS] token output embedding is used for the text representation.
To avoid information leak, a unimodal self-attention mask is used, where the queries and text are not allowed to see each other.
The highest pairwise similarity between each query output and the text representation is selected as the image-text similarity.
The Image-Text Matching (ITM) objective in the BLIP-2 model controls the interaction between query tokens and text tokens by using a causal self-attention mask.
This mask allows queries to attend to each other but not the text tokens.
Each text token can attend to all queries and its previous text tokens.
This is similar to the one used in UniLM (Dong et al., 2019).
The purpose of this design is to allow the model to focus on the relevant parts of the text and image during the learning process.
Vision-language representation learning is important for BLIP-2's second-stage vision-to-language generative learning because it reduces the burden on the LLM to learn vision-language alignment.
Without representation learning, the Q-Former fails to bridge the modality gap effectively, leading to significantly lower performance on zero-shot VQA (Visual Question Answering).
This is similar to the Perceiver Resampler in Flamingo, where without representation learning, both types of LLMs give substantially lower performance on zero-shot VQA.
In particular, OPT suffers from catastrophic forgetting where performance drastically degrades as training proceeds.
BLIP-2 outperforms Flamingo by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2, while using 54x fewer trainable parameters.

Vision Transformer (ViT) represents an image as an input sequence for a standard Transformer encoder by splitting the image into fixed-size patches, linearly embedding each patch, adding position embeddings, and feeding the resulting sequence of vectors to the Transformer encoder.

The number of patches is determined by the resolution of the original image, the number of channels, the resolution of each image patch, and the effective input sequence length for the Transformer, which is the number of patches.
The position embeddings are learnable 1D embeddings that retain positional information.
The resulting sequence of embedding vectors serves as input to the encoder.

In ViT (Vision Transformer), the image patches are converted into the input embeddings used by the Transformer encoder through a series of steps:
The image is split into fixed-size patches.
The size of each patch is (P, P), and the number of patches (N) is equal to the resulting number of patches, which also serves as the effective input sequence length for the Transformer.
Each patch is linearly embedded to D dimensions, where D is the constant latent vector size used throughout the Transformer's layers.
This linear projection is performed using a trainable linear projection (Eq. 1).
A learnable embedding, referred to as the [class] embedding, is prepended to the sequence of embedded patches.
Position embeddings are added to the patch embeddings to retain positional information.
These position embeddings are standard learnable 1D position embeddings.
The resulting sequence of embedding vectors serves as input to the Transformer encoder.

It's important to note that the Transformer encoder consists of alternating layers of multi-headed self-attention (MSA) and MLP blocks, with layer normalization (LN) applied before every block and residual connections after every block.

The purpose of the learnable class token in the Vision Transformer architecture is to serve as the image representation for classification.
During both pre-training and fine-tuning, a classification head is attached to the z° (the state of the learnable class token at the output of the Transformer encoder).
The classification head is implemented by a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with one hidden layer at pre-training time and by a single linear layer at fine-tuning time.

This is necessary because the Transformer encoder operates on patch-level embeddings and before feeding the inputs to the Transformer encoder.
The positional embeddings carry no information about the 2D positions of the patches and all spatial relations between the patches have to be learned from scratch.
This is done to encode the spatial information as instead of their absolute position.

The standard Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture introduces an image-specific inductive bias compared to convolutional neural networks (CNNs) primarily at the patch extraction step.
This is where the image is split into fixed-size patches.
After that, the ViT architecture processes the image as a sequence of patches using a standard Transformer encoder, which is originally designed for natural language processing tasks.
Unlike CNNs, ViT does not rely on convolutional layers for local feature processing.

However, it should be noted that the pre-trained position embeddings may no longer be meaningful, and for that reason, 2D interpolation of the pre-trained position embeddings is performed according to their location in the original image.
This is the only point at which an inductive bias about the 2D structure of the images is manually injected into the Vision Transformer.

However, it does mention that ViT performs well on most recognition benchmarks at a lower pre-training cost compared to ResNets, but it overfits more on smaller datasets.
For larger datasets, ViT performs better and overtakes ResNets.
The text also mentions that larger ViT variants perform better with larger pre-training datasets.
Therefore, while ViT may not strictly require large-scale pre-training, it seems to benefit from it, especially on larger datasets.

The hybrid ResNet-ViT model differs from the standard ViT model in how it produces the input representations for the Transformer by processing inputs in a 2-dimensional shape, instead of a 1-dimensional sequence of patches.
It also incorporates Axial Transformer blocks, in which instead of a self-attention followed by an MLP, there is a row-self-attention plus an MLP followed by a column-self-attention plus an MLP.
This is different from the standard ViT model which processes inputs as a 1-D sequence of patches and uses standard self-attention and MLP blocks.

CLIP stands for Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining.
It is a model that learns to understand the relationship between images and text by being trained on a large dataset of paired images and captions.
The model is designed to learn transferable visual representations that can be used for a wide variety of downstream tasks.

CLIP attempts to address the limitation of traditional supervised image classification by learning from natural language supervision, as it aims to overcome the need for large-scale, manually annotated image datasets.
Instead, it learns visual models directly from text descriptions, which can be more readily available and easier to obtain.
CLIP uses a large-scale internet dataset for pre-training.
The size of the dataset introduced in the paper is not explicitly mentioned, but it is stated that it contains more than 400 million image-text pairs.
During pre-training, CLIP learns to associate images with their corresponding textual descriptions by performing a single dot product in a learned joint embedding space.
This means that the model learns to represent both images and text in a shared space, where similar images and text are closer together and dissimilar ones are further apart.
This allows the model to understand the relationship between the two domains and perform tasks such as image classification, object detection, and captioning based on natural language prompts.
In CLIP, the image encoder is responsible for computing a feature representation for an image, acting as the computer vision backbone.
The text encoder, on the other hand, generates the weights of a linear classifier based on the text, which specifies the visual concepts that the classes represent.

During CLIP's training, image and text representations are compared in a contrastive learning manner.
The model is trained to maximize the similarity between an image and its corresponding text description while minimizing the similarity between the image and unrelated text descriptions.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a model designed to address the problem of knowledge-intensive NLP tasks.

It is a unified architecture that incorporates retrieval to improve performance across several tasks such as open-domain question answering, fact checking, fact completion, long-form question answering, Wikipedia article generation, dialogue, translation, and language modeling.
The model uses retrieved documents to enhance its understanding and generate more accurate responses.
The RAG architecture uses two types of memory: non-parametric memory and latent documents.
Non-parametric memory: This is the main memory of the RAG model, which stores the retrieved documents.
It plays a crucial role in providing context and facts for the model to generate answers.
Latent documents: These are additional documents retrieved during the inference phase to help the model generate more accurate answers.
The number of latent documents can be adjusted at test time, affecting performance and runtime.

Using an external non-parametric memory makes RAG easier to update with new knowledge than a purely parametric language model because non-parametric models like RAG can easily update their knowledge at test time, while parametric-only models like T5 or BART require further training to update their behavior as the world changes.

This is because non-parametric models store specific knowledge in their memory, and this knowledge can be easily updated or replaced, whereas parametric models learn to generate responses based on the parameters learned during training, and updating these parameters requires additional training data and computational resources.

BERT stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers.
The main idea behind the model is to pre-train deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers.
This allows the model to better understand the context and semantics of the text, leading to improved performance on a wide range of natural language processing tasks.

BERT uses a bidirectional Transformer, which means it considers both the left and right context when processing a sentence, while OpenAI GPT uses a left-to-right Transformer, which only considers the left context.
This bidirectionality in BERT allows it to capture more contextual information and improve its performance.

The masked language model (MLM) objective used during BERT pre-training is a procedure where a random subset of words in a sentence are masked, and the model is trained to predict the masked words based on the context provided by the surrounding words.
This is done to improve the model's language understanding capability.

The masked language model (MLM) allows BERT to learn bidirectional representations while a traditional left-to-right language model cannot because the MLM randomly masks some words in a sentence and requires the model to predict the masked words based on the context, encouraging the model to understand the sentence as a whole and learn bidirectional relationships between words.

In contrast, a traditional left-to-right language model only considers the words in the order they appear in the sentence, limiting its ability to understand the context and learn bidirectional relationships.
The purpose of the Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) task in BERT is to predict whether a given sentence is the next sentence in a text, or a random sentence.
This task is used during the pre-training phase of BERT to help the model understand the order and coherence of sentences in a text.
During BERT pre-training, 50% of the time the second sampled text span is the actual next sentence, and 50% of the time it is a randomly selected sentence.

BERT, OpenAI GPT, and ELMo differ in their approaches to obtaining contextual representations as follows:
BERT and OpenAI GPT are fine-tuning approaches, while ELMo is a feature-based approach.
This means that BERT and OpenAI GPT start with pre-trained models and further adapt them to specific tasks, while ELMo generates representations directly from the input text without pre-training.
BERT and OpenAI GPT are both pre-trained on large text corpora using transformer-based models.
However, BERT is trained on both left and right context in all layers, while OpenAI GPT is a left-to-right Transformer LM.
BERT learns special symbols like [SEP], [CLS] and sentence A/B embeddings during pre-training, while OpenAI GPT only introduces these symbols at fine-tuning time.
